headline: High: Windsurf’s shared filesystem, clipboard, MCP, and auto-execute paths create dangerous prompt-injection, leakage, and cascading-action risks with Plane’s file/task inputs.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Windsurf can read workspace files, clipboard, and MCP content, and may auto-execute commands; Plane accepts file uploads and hyperlinks and touches notes/tasks/issues. That creates a plausible bridge where attacker-controlled Plane content can be copied or synced into Windsurf and treated as instructions. Plane lacks isolation controls; Windsurf’s permissive tool-use surface raises the risk.
conditions: IF Plane content is copied into Windsurf clipboard or workspace files without sanitization, injection is possible.
IF Windsurf auto-execute is enabled, malicious instructions in imported content can trigger tool use.
mitigations: Disable Windsurf auto-execute.
Keep Plane exports out of the shared workspace.
Use a manual review step before pasting Plane content into Windsurf.
Restrict MCP servers to trusted, read-only endpoints.
requires-engineering: add provenance tagging for imported content.

B_data_leakage.rationale: Plane handles issues, tasks, roadmaps, files, images, and hyperlinks, while Windsurf reads workspace files and sends context through a model proxy/MCP with broad network egress. If both touch the same workspace or copied files, sensitive Plane data can flow into Windsurf and then to third-party inference paths. The pair lacks documented isolation between them.
conditions: IF Plane files or notes are placed in Windsurf’s workspace, those contents can be ingested by Windsurf.
IF Windsurf routes context through its model proxy or MCP, copied Plane data may leave the local machine.
mitigations: Do not place Plane exports in Windsurf workspaces.
Use separate OS accounts or directories for the two tools.
Disable or tightly scope MCP servers.
Review and redact sensitive Plane attachments before transfer.
requires-engineering: enforce workspace-level data-loss controls.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Plane is write_filesystem false, but Windsurf can write_filesystem, modify_git_state, and use shared local filesystem state across instances. The main conflict is not between two writers to the same dir from Plane, but between Windsurf instances and any shared workspace artifacts originating from Plane. Because Plane itself cannot write, the conflict is narrower than high, though still real in default editor workflows.
conditions: IF multiple Windsurf instances operate on the same local workspace, file and git conflicts can occur.
IF Plane-generated files are manually copied into the shared workspace, Windsurf may overwrite them.
mitigations: Use one Windsurf instance per workspace.
Avoid editing Plane-exported files in parallel.
Commit or stash git changes before launching another session.
Separate generated artifacts into per-agent directories.
requires-engineering: add locking around shared workspace writes.

D_cascading_error.rationale: Windsurf can act on tool output and modify git state or execute shell commands, while Plane produces issues, tasks, roadmaps, files, and notes that may be treated as authoritative work items. If Plane output is imported into Windsurf without verification, Windsurf can turn a mistaken task or file into code or commits. That is a direct action-taking cascade with potentially irreversible effects.
conditions: IF Plane output is used as input to Windsurf without human verification, erroneous tasks can become code changes or shell actions.
IF Windsurf auto-execute is enabled, the cascade can happen without an approval pause.
mitigations: Require human review before Windsurf acts on Plane output.
Disable auto-execute in Windsurf.
Use a checklist for task-to-code translation.
Limit git writes to reviewed branches only.
requires-engineering: add verification gates between task intake and execution.

E_compliance.rationale: Plane is an open-source issue/task system with file uploads, while Windsurf is a closed-source coding agent that handles model-provider keys and broad network egress. The pair can move the same data class through different retention and residency regimes, but the profiles do not document a specific residency or certification mismatch. Uncertainty therefore stays at medium rather than low.
conditions: IF regulated data from Plane is copied into Windsurf, the data may enter a different retention or processing regime.
IF Windsurf is configured with a non-compliant model provider, compliance obligations may be breached.
mitigations: Avoid moving regulated data from Plane into Windsurf.
Confirm provider and retention settings in Windsurf.
Document which data classes may cross the boundary.
Use separate tenants or projects for regulated work.
requires-engineering: implement residency and retention policy enforcement.
